boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Sewell's Point record (May 18-19, 1861) in Blockade of the Chesapeake Bay [May-June 1861]. The blockade of Hampton Roads and the reinforcement of the Norfolk posts are context. Campaign-wide movements, reinforcements, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads 'Two gunboats [US]; battery garrison [CS]'; the live field reads zero. Gwynn says the Monticello carried three guns, one a heavy 10-inch Dahlgren, joined on the 18th by a steam tug with one gun, and that by 5 p.m. on the 19th three 32-pounders and two small rifled guns were in the battery with detachments of infantry and artillery. Eagle says the battery was masked with thirteen embrasures and that the Confederates had three rifled cannon.
claims.rationale: Vessel and gun counts, not personnel; the two reports differ on the battery's guns. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: The frozen commanders are Brigadier General Walter Gwynn and Captain Peyton Colquitt for the Confederates and Lieutenant D.L. Braine (navy) for the Union; the live page lists Braine and Gwynn. Gwynn says he gave Colquitt command of all forces and guns at the post and returned to Norfolk before the May 19 fire. Eagle signs as commanding the Star [Monticello] and says Braine had charge of the pivot gun.
claims.rationale: Roles from the two reports: the listed Union commander appears as the pivot-gun officer under Eagle. No listed commander receives automatic sole credit.

Gwynn says the Monticello was driven off after an hour and a half and that her retreat showed the fire had become too warm; Eagle says the action lasted one hour and fifteen minutes and that he withdrew only for want of ammunition.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit.

open_questions: Colquitt's May 19 report, Stringham's May 19 report, Braine's May 22 statement on the Thomas Freeborn and Dahlgren's May 30 report on shell fragments were read but not selected; the May 18 exchange is recorded only in Gwynn's account.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. Gwynn's May 20, 1861 telegram and report (Army Official Records Series I, Volume II) are one family of interested Confederate accounts. Eagle's May 19 report (Navy Official Records Series I, Volume 5) is one family of interested Union accounts. The Army and Navy Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses, and reprints of a report in the other compilation are copies. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge. No Scribner history narrates this engagement; Nicolay's The Outbreak of Rebellion mentions Great Bethel only in passing.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
